title: New York's New Medically Assisted Aid In Dying Law Will Be Used to Kill The Mentally Ill
subtitle: Other countries are doing it already.
body_html:
“If you aren’t sure as to what decision to make, always err on the side of the patient”.

—Jeffrey Curtis, MD

I don't love medical-assisted aid-in-dying for one specific reason. Wherever MAiD has been implemented, it’s been used to end the lives of the most vulnerable people, a predictable fallout from the utter failure of psychiatry to do its job.

The state in which I used to live, and in which I still practice medicine, is New York State. It just passed a medically-assisted aid-in-dying law.

Ironically, in cases of the terminally ill from non-psychiatric illness, I’m overwhelmingly in favor of patient autonomy and the physician-patient relationship leading the way. I shudder to think of other people trapped in lives of endless horror and suffering.

In the state of New York, the candidates for NY-MAiD include the following:

17.  “TERMINAL  ILLNESS OR CONDITION” MEANS AN INCURABLE AND IRREVERS-
 IBLE ILLNESS OR CONDITION THAT HAS BEEN MEDICALLY  CONFIRMED  AND  WILL,
 WITHIN REASONABLE MEDICAL JUDGMENT, PRODUCE DEATH WITHIN SIX MONTHS.

This leaves the door wide open to chronically suicidal individuals, for whom psychiatric medications haven't helped. Many of those individuals will have personality disorders, for which suicidality is a common symptom. I think we're making a mistake by not excluding primary psychiatric disorders as a rationale for death by a doctor.

I get that this isn’t the intent of that law. This is always intended to be used only in extreme cases; more people are terminally ill, and then it expands to others whose suffering is tremendous, but not terminal in the traditional sense of the term. That's what happens in the real world. Let’s look at what’s happening elsewhere in the world, to peer into the future:

The NYS law is more restrictive (now) than Canada’s criteria, passed in 2016:

The Act permits medical aid in dying for patients who meet all of the following criteria, i.e the patient:

(1) is an insured person within the meaning of the Health Insurance Act;

(2) is of full age and capable of giving consent to care;

(3) is at the end of life;

(4) suffers from an incurable serious illness;

(5) suffers from an advanced state of irreversible decline in capability; and

(6) suffers from constant and unbearable physical or psychological pain which cannot be relieved in a manner the person deems tolerable.

However, I suspect there will be a problem, and I'm going to use some data to back it up. It always starts carefully, restricted, and framed as rare. Then, it ramps up. Let’s look at the numbers from the Netherlands:

As people got used to the new law, the number of Dutch people being euthanised began to rise sharply, from under 2,000 in 2007 to almost 6,600 in 2017. (Around the same number are estimated to have had their euthanasia request turned down as not conforming with the legal requirements.) Also in 2017, some 1,900 Dutch people killed themselves, while the number of people who died under palliative sedation – in theory, succumbing to their illness while cocooned from physical discomfort, but in practice often dying of dehydration while unconscious – hit an astonishing 32,000. Altogether, well over a quarter of all deaths in 2017 in the Netherlands were induced.

In Canada, in 2024, it is the 5th leading cause of death:

Medically-assisted dying – also known as voluntary euthanasia – accounted for 4.7% of deaths in Canada in 2023, new government data shows.

The country’s fifth annual report since euthanasia was legalised in 2016 showed around 15,300 people underwent assisted dying last year after being successful in their applications.

It’s disproportionately white people choosing MAiD, at least in Canada:

Around 96% of recipients identified as white people, who account for about 70% of Canada's population. It is unclear what caused this disparity.

And more data that suggest it's not being used in an equitable or medical-condition-driven fashion, and more by cultural variation, comes from the vast differences in use of MAID across different regions of Canada:

Assisted dying continued to have the highest usage rate in Quebec, which accounted for nearly 37% of all euthanasia deaths, despite the province holding just 22% of Canada's population.

The enlightened Dutch have had MAiD longer than most, since 2012.

We have one cohort study, which looked at the outcomes of individuals requesting medical assistance in dying based on psychiatric suffering, only among the young (those under 24).

The study included 397 processed applications submitted by 353 individuals (73.4% female; mean [SD] age, 20.84 [1.90] years).

The time frame was from:

Between 2012 and the first half of 2021, the number of MAID-PS applications by young patients increased from 10 to 39.

It's not a tidal wave. What were the outcomes?

The most likely outcome was application retracted by the patient (188 [47.3%]) followed by application rejected (178 [44.8%]).

The overwhelming majority of these individuals did not end up receiving aid in dying, by a physician, giving them drugs with which to kill themselves.

Let’s dig into their results, from this primary psychiatric sample, in more detail:

For 12 applications (3.0%), patients died by MAID. Seventeen applications (4.3%) were stopped because the patient died by suicide during the application process, and 2 (0.5%) because the patient died after they voluntarily stopped eating and drinking. All patients who died by suicide or MAID (n = 29) had multiple psychiatric diagnoses (most frequently major depression, autism spectrum disorder, personality disorders, eating disorder, and/or trauma-related disorder) and extensive treatment histories. Twenty-eight of these patients (96.5%) had a history of suicidality that included multiple suicide attempts prior to the MAID application. Among 17 patients who died by suicide, 13 of 14 (92.9%) had a history of crisis-related hospital admission, and 9 of 12 patients who died by MAID (75.0%) had a history of self-harm.1

Only 3% of the hundreds of individuals who applied were approved and granted MAiD.

More individuals completed suicide in the process than were able to wait till the end of the process.

This is horrifying. Here's an additional horrifying detail from this study:

Those who died by MAID or suicide were mostly female and had long treatment histories and prominent suicidality. These findings suggest that there is an urgent need for more knowledge about persistent death wishes and effective suicide prevention strategies for this high-risk group.

We're killing traumatized women, or reducing the conceptual barriers to death by suicide. No amount of good intentions is gonna change the fact that hundreds of additional applicants—recall, this only included those 24 and under—had to go through the process of being evaluated for the death they craved, and we declined that relief.

97% individuals thought they were going to have help with their suicide, and 4.3% of the cohort died by suicide in the process. The base rate of death by suicide in borderline personality disorder, for example, is on the order of 5%. Adding MAiD to the roster increases the rate of individuals who die in their youth.

This is especially galling because borderline personality disorder, although a severe and disabling condition, more often leads to remission than death. Mary Zanarini and colleagues, in the McLean Study of Adult Development, the largest longitudinal study of BPD, note several key findings in their 6-year follow-up paper:

The first finding is that remissions are far more common than previously recognized (about 74%). The second is that these remissions are quite stable and thus, recurrences are quite rare (about 6%). The third finding is that completed suicides are far more rare than anticipated (about 4% vs. 10%).2

The study has now gone on for over 26 years. The overwhelming majority of patients no longer need criteria for borderline personality disorder after 10 years, at 85%, and 99% of those who don't die by suicide, which caps out at around 5%, will remit over 26 years, with a 15% relapse rate.3

Even severe suicidality, presenting in youth, no matter how traumatized, personality disordered, and vulnerable, on average, relents. When we allow MAiD in psychiatric populations, more die than would otherwise, at least in the Netherlands. We already have data from Canada suggesting strong cultural and socioeconomic variability, not based on terminal illness or other objective criteria.

Dear readers, I want you to imagine the hundreds of people who are going to apply for assistance, and try, beg, insist to their doctors that they can't live for another six months. It really is terminal. Many of these patients have attempted suicide already. Many of their doctors have stuck with them throughout many suicide attempts. Our efforts to insist that life is worth living, and there's no way we can help them end it? My arguments, in those crucial moments, are undercut by this law.

We can decide, as a society, if we'd rather have more options at the end of our lives, at the expense of the young and vulnerable. Maybe that's a trade-off we want to make.

Maybe we want subject physicians to these requests? Maybe we feel that's worth it. Maybe we want physicians to decide whether death is the best option, and whether we should help? As someone who is a psychiatrist for individuals who are routinely suicidal, I have little interest in helping them qualify for death when I could be championing a life worth living.

People killed themselves all the time. Suicide is increasing. More people are gonna die by their own choosing if they don't have to do it for themselves, and maybe that's more humane. It's probably more humane for some, and more lethal for others.

My concern, as a physician, is that I want to spend my limited time helping people find lives they want to live, rather than looking for legal criteria on their way out the door. This law allocates physician time to grim decisions, not hopeful encounters. And, perhaps more importantly, we haven't had an honest conversation about the trade-off we are making.

We're not saying out loud the quiet part—we're gonna consign, traumatized women with autism, personality disorders, depression, and other forms of psychological suffering that, overwhelmingly, we as a society have chosen to inflict upon them, well, while not holding the perpetrators accountable. We live in a society full of redacted Epstein files, not accountable perpetrators. But to make sure that all of us with access to health insurance have a smooth and easy exit, not marked by that or remarkable suffering. At the end, we're willing to feed the most vulnerable, overwhelmingly young women, into the maw of death, without a conversation; that's what we're doing.

There are no firm barriers against subjecting chronically suicidal individuals to early death. There are no frank conversations about the risk. These provisions are included in the law, and there are limitations on who can be held accountable.

Keep in mind, while we are allowing medical-assisted dying, we're still holding physicians accountable for medical malpractice for not preventing suicide in patients at extremely high risk. We indemnify those who assist in death, in this law, and for those who champion life? Medical malpractice claims await.

This is a farce, gruesome, and the opposite of a good idea.

All of this having been said, nobody wants to die in pain, unable to escape that pain, when it's obvious that's likely to happen—I include myself in that number. I've already had this kind of talk with my mother, and she had this talk with my father before his death as well. We want a more compassionate world, where nobody dies in horrific pain.

But the fact that we approved MAiD before we made psychedelic medicines legal? We approved spending time dithering about suicide assistance before we provided broad insurance coverage for everyone to have access to accelerated Transcranial magnetic stimulation, with its 90% response rates? We're helping people die, before we're willing to help them live, free of that pain.

I had ChatGPT help with a table of available treatments for suicidality (none of which are required to be administered before MAiD is considered, and most are not covered by insurance broadly). I even checked all the references to make sure they aren’t made up.

4

This will end as poorly as it has in every other place it's been implemented. It may be a decision, a series of trade-offs, we're comfortable with, but we haven't been frank enough with ourselves to have that conversation.

If legislators want a recommendation, I'll make some:

  1. We should exclude anybody with a prior suicide attempt from the process.

  2. We should exclude all those with no co-occurring medical condition

  3. We should exclude those who have chronic suicidality before the onset of their terminal illness.

  4. We should exclude borderline personality disorder, absence of other life-threatening illnesses, and

  5. We should include more physician signatures necessary on any patient with a known psychiatric illness for aid in death, on par with the four signatures that are necessary in the state of New York to commit someone under a “2-PC” involuntary commitment.

Before we spend time and energy on death, we should be saving lives. Say it with me: Broad insurance coverage for life-saving psychiatric treatment now, please.

At a bare minimum, it will reduce the spending on physician suicide assessments.
